text: Over the last few decades, public interest in hunger artists has dwindled sharply, and an exhibition of fasting that once filled a showmans pockets would today attract hardly anyone at all. <break time="0.8s" /> There was a time, however, when the whole town took part in the spectacle, and as the fast went on, people came daily, some buying season tickets to sit before the little barred cage all day long. <break time="0.8s" /> Even at night visitors came to view him by torchlight, and on fine days the cage was carried into the open air, where the children above all stared at him in open mouthed wonder. <break time="0.8s" /> To the adults he was often just a fashionable joke, but the children, holding hands for safety, gazed in amazement at the pale figure in black tights, his ribs sticking out sharply, sitting on the scattered straw. <break time="0.8s" /> Scorning even a chair, he sometimes nodded politely and answered questions with a strained smile, or he stretched an arm through the bars so that people could feel how thin it was, before sinking back into himself again. <break time="0.8s" /> Then he would ignore everyone, even the striking of the clock that was the cages only furniture, and simply stare ahead with half closed eyes, now and then sipping water from a tiny glass to moisten his lips. <break time="0.8s" /> Besides the changing crowds, there were also permanent watchers chosen by the public, usually butchers, oddly enough, who in teams of three kept their eyes on him day and night so that he could not secretly take any food. <break time="0.8s" /> This was, however, merely a formality introduced to reassure the masses, for those who understood the art knew well that during his fast the hunger artist would never swallow even the smallest crumb, not even if forced.
